==Problem 24==
For some positive integers <imath>p</imath>, there is a quadrilateral <imath>ABCD</imath> with positive integer side lengths, perimeter <imath>p</imath>, right angles at <imath>B</imath> and <imath>C</imath>, <imath>AB=2</imath>, and <imath>CD=AD</imath>.  How many different values of <imath>p<2015</imath> are possible?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }30\qquad\textbf{(B) }31\qquad\textbf{(C) }61\qquad\textbf{(D) }62\qquad\textbf{(E) }63</imath>



==Solution 1==
Let <imath>BC = x</imath> and <imath>CD = AD = y</imath> be positive integers. Drop a perpendicular from <imath>A</imath> to <imath>CD</imath> to show that, using the Pythagorean Theorem, that
<cmath>x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = y^2.</cmath>
Simplifying yields <imath>x^2 - 4y + 4 = 0</imath>, so <imath>x^2 = 4(y - 1)</imath>. Thus, <imath>y</imath> is one more than a perfect square.

The perimeter <imath>p = 2 + x + 2y = 2y + 2\sqrt{y - 1} + 2</imath> must be less than 2015. Simple calculations demonstrate that <imath>y = 31^2 + 1 = 962</imath> is valid, but <imath>y = 32^2 + 1 = 1025</imath> is not. On the lower side, <imath>y = 1</imath> does not work (because <imath>x > 0</imath>), but <imath>y = 1^2 + 1</imath> does work. Hence, there are 31 valid <imath>y</imath> (all <imath>y</imath> such that <imath>y = n^2 + 1</imath> for <imath>1 \le n \le 31</imath>), and so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 31}</imath>

==Solution 2==
Let <imath>BC = x</imath> and <imath>CD = AD = z</imath> be positive integers. Drop a perpendicular from <imath>A</imath> to <imath>CD</imath>. Denote the intersection point of the perpendicular and <imath>CD</imath> as <imath>E</imath>.

<imath>AE</imath>'s length is <imath>x</imath>, as well.
Call <imath>ED</imath> <imath>y</imath>.
By the Pythagorean Theorem,  <imath>x^2 + y^2 = (y + 2)^2</imath>.
And so: <imath>x^2 = 4y + 4</imath>, or <imath>y = (x^2-4)/4</imath>.

Writing this down and testing, it appears that this holds for all <imath>x</imath>. However, since there is a dividend of 4, the numerator must be divisible by 4 to conform to the criteria that the side lengths are positive integers.
In effect, <imath>x</imath> must be a multiple of 2 to let the side lengths be integers. We test, and soon reach 62. It gives us <imath>p = 1988</imath>, which is less than 2015. However, 64 gives us <imath>2116 > 2015</imath>, so we know 62 is the largest we can go up to. Count all the even numbers from 2 to 62, and we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 31}</imath>.

-jackshi2006

==Solution 3 (Less Counting)==
Let <imath>BC = n</imath> and <imath>CD = AD = m</imath> be positive integers. Drop a perpendicular from <imath>A</imath> to <imath>CD</imath>. Denote the intersection point of the perpendicular and <imath>CD</imath> as <imath>E</imath>.

<imath>AE</imath>'s length is <imath>n</imath>, and <imath>ED = m-2</imath>
By the Pythagorean Theorem,  <imath>m^2 = (m-2)^2 + n^2</imath>
, therefore <imath>n^2 = 4(m-1)</imath>

Notice that 4 is already a perfect square and <imath>n</imath> is an integer, meaning <imath>m-1</imath> also has to be a perfect square. 
We can denote <imath>m-1</imath> as <imath>x^2</imath>, therefore we have <imath>m = x^2 + 1</imath>, <imath>n = 2x</imath>, and each <imath>x</imath> will correspond to a pair of <imath>(n, m)</imath>. 

Since <imath>p<2015</imath>, <imath>2 + n + m + m<2015</imath> which gives us <imath>n+2m<2013</imath>. Substituting <imath>x</imath> will give us <imath>2x+2(x^2 + 1) < 2013</imath>, simplify this will again give us <imath>x^2 + x + 1 < 1006.5</imath>
Try <imath>x = 32</imath>, <imath>x^2 + x + 1 = 1057 > 1006.5</imath>, exceeded
so <imath>x</imath> must be less than <imath>32</imath>

When <imath>x=31</imath>, <imath>x^2 + x + 1 = 993 < 1006.5</imath>, <imath>x=31</imath> works for us.

For <imath>x</imath> in <imath>(0, \infty)</imath>, <imath>f(x) = x^2 + x + 1</imath> increases, therefore for any <imath>x<31</imath>, <imath>f(x) < f(31) < 1006.5</imath>

Thus, any <imath>x</imath> in <imath>[1, 31]</imath> satisfy the condition that <imath>x^2 + x + 1 < 1006.5</imath>. <imath>x</imath> needs to be integer, and there are <imath>31</imath> integers in the interval <imath>[1, 31]</imath>. 

Each <imath>x</imath> corresponds to a <imath>(n, m)</imath>, meaning there are <imath>31</imath> possible value for different pairs of <imath>(n, m)</imath> and lead to <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 31}</imath> possible values for the perimeter <imath>p</imath>.
